title: Croup and Paediatric Stridor: Severity Assessment and Escalation

evidenceAudit.scope: PAEDIATRIC topic. Children aged about 6 months to 8 years with croup (viral laryngotracheitis) in the emergency department (ED) or clinic: severity grading, red flags for other causes of stridor, oral dexamethasone, nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine), observation, admission and paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) or anaesthesia escalation. Uses the Canadian Paediatric Society (CPS) 2026 practice point, the Children's Minnesota 2025 croup guideline and product labels. Infants under 6 months, recurrent or atypical croup, known airway anomalies and adults are excluded.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-21.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi croup guideline was found.

Both main sources are North American; local availability of racemic adrenaline varies; L-adrenaline 1:1000 is used where racemic is unavailable (CPS 2026, Section Epinephrine). Check hospital formulary.
Children's Minnesota writes the racemic adrenaline dose as 0.5 mg; CPS gives 0.5 mL of racemic adrenaline. The CPS volume is used and the difference is flagged for pharmacy review.
The dexamethasone product information opened is for an adult 10 mg/5 mL strength; paediatric dose comes from CPS 2026 and Children's Minnesota 2025.
Typical oxygen saturation and respiratory rate ranges by age are not from these sources.

pathophysiology.summary: Croup is caused by viruses, most often parainfluenza types 1 and 3; influenza, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus and SARS-CoV-2 also cause it (CPS 2026, Section Etiology and pathophysiology). Inflammation and oedema narrow the subglottic airway and cause upper airway obstruction (CPS 2026, Section Etiology and pathophysiology). Corticosteroids reduce symptoms from 2 to 3 hours after one oral dose, lasting 24 to 48 hours (CPS 2026, Section Corticosteroids). Nebulised adrenaline improves distress within 10 to 30 minutes, lasting at least 1 hour and gone by 2 hours (CPS 2026, Section Epinephrine).

symptoms: Sudden barky cough, hoarse voice, inspiratory stridor and breathing difficulty (CPS 2026, Section Clinical presentation).
Preceding cold symptoms; often worse at night (CPS 2026, Section Clinical presentation).
Symptoms usually last 3 to 7 days; cough settles within 48 hours in 60% (CPS 2026, Section Clinical presentation).
physicalSigns: Mild: occasional cough, no or minimal stridor at rest, no or mild in-drawing (CPS 2026, Table 2).
Moderate: frequent cough, stridor easily heard at rest, in-drawing at rest, little or no agitation (CPS 2026, Table 2).
Severe: prominent stridor, marked in-drawing, substantial agitation or lethargy (CPS 2026, Table 2).
Impending respiratory failure: quieter stridor, lethargy or reduced consciousness, dusky or cyanosed without oxygen (CPS 2026, Table 2).
redFlags: Toxic appearance, drooling or difficulty swallowing: consider epiglottitis, abscess or tracheitis (CPS 2026, Section Differential diagnosis and Table 1).
Oxygen saturation below 92% on air: emergency evaluation (Children's Minnesota croup guideline 2025, Page 1).
Severe distress or impending failure not responding to treatment: refer to PICU or anaesthesia (CPS 2026, Section Treatment).
Age under 6 months, recurrent, prolonged or very severe croup: look for airway narrowing (CPS 2026, Section Differential diagnosis).
precipitants: Parainfluenza virus types 1 and 3 (CPS 2026, Section Etiology and pathophysiology).
Influenza A and B, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, metapneumovirus (CPS 2026, Section Etiology and pathophysiology).
SARS-CoV-2 omicron variant (CPS 2026, Section Etiology and pathophysiology).
Autumn and winter peaks (CPS 2026, Section Clinical presentation).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: High fever, toxic appearance, poor response to nebulised adrenaline (CPS 2026, Table 1).
No barky cough, sudden high fever, drooling, anxious, sitting forward in sniffing position (CPS 2026, Table 1).
Fever, neck pain, sore throat, dysphagia, then torticollis and drooling (CPS 2026, Table 1).
Choking episode, biphasic stridor, wheeze, reduced air entry (CPS 2026, Table 1).
Rapid dysphagia, wheeze, stridor, urticaria (CPS 2026, Table 1).

clinicalManagement.title: Keep the child calm and assess
actions: Keep the child with the carer and avoid frightening procedures (CPS 2026, Section General care).
Grade severity with CPS Table 2 and check saturation (CPS 2026, Table 2; Children's Minnesota 2025, Page 1).
Look for red flags of epiglottitis, abscess, tracheitis, foreign body or anaphylaxis (CPS 2026, Table 1).

clinicalManagement.title: Give dexamethasone to every child
actions: Give oral dexamethasone (see Medicines) for mild to severe croup (CPS 2026, Section Corticosteroids).
Do not use humidified air or mist tents (CPS 2026, Section General care).
Antipyretics help fever and discomfort (CPS 2026, Section General care).

clinicalManagement.title: Nebulised adrenaline for moderate or severe croup
actions: Give nebulised adrenaline (see Medicines) (CPS 2026, Section Epinephrine).
Monitor up to 2 hours for repeat doses (Children's Minnesota croup guideline 2025, Page 1).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate severe or failing cases
actions: Refer to PICU or anaesthesia when severe distress or impending failure responds poorly (CPS 2026, Section Treatment).
Ear, nose and throat (ENT) consultation if symptoms stay severe despite treatment (CPS 2026, Section Other therapies).
Heliox may be used occasionally in severe cases to avoid intubation but is not routine (CPS 2026, Section Heliox).
Antibiotics and salbutamol are rarely indicated (CPS 2026, Section Other therapies).

clinicalManagement.title: Admit or discharge
actions: Discharge if symptoms do not recur 2 to 4 hours after adrenaline (CPS 2026, Section Epinephrine).

Consider admission after 3 or more adrenaline doses in 24 hours, or 2 doses with ongoing work of breathing, dehydration, barriers to follow-up or high parental anxiety (Children's Minnesota croup guideline 2025, Notes 2 and 5).
Admit critically ill, hypoxic or toxic-looking children (Children's Minnesota croup guideline 2025, Note 5).

regimens.dose: PAEDIATRIC: 0.6 mg/kg orally as a single dose (CPS croup practice point 2026, Section Corticosteroids); maximum 12 mg (Children's Minnesota croup guideline 2025, Page 1). Intramuscular route if persistent vomiting or significant distress (CPS 2026, Section Corticosteroids).
regimens.route: Oral; intramuscular if vomiting or significant distress
regimens.duration: One dose is enough for most children; consider a further dose only if more than 24 hours since the last (Children's Minnesota croup guideline 2025, Page 1)
adjustments: The 10 mg/5 mL solution is not indicated for children (Dexamethasone SmPC, Section 4.2); use a paediatric-appropriate product from the hospital formulary.
Lower doses of 0.15 to 0.3 mg/kg have unclear equivalence (CPS 2026, Section Corticosteroids).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Clinical response from 2 to 3 hours after the dose (CPS 2026, Section Corticosteroids).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to dexamethasone or excipients (Dexamethasone SmPC, Section 4.3).
Systemic infection unless treated (Dexamethasone SmPC, Section 4.3).
Caution after chickenpox or measles exposure in immunosuppressed children (Dexamethasone SmPC, Section 4.4).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Barky cough, inspiratory stridor and hoarseness after a cold, age 6 months to 3 years most often (CPS 2026, Section Clinical presentation).
Mild, moderate, severe or impending respiratory failure by cough, stridor, in-drawing, agitation or lethargy and cyanosis (CPS 2026, Table 2).
No recurrence of symptoms 2 to 4 hours after treatment (CPS 2026, Section Epinephrine).

teaching.scope: PAEDIATRIC topic. Children aged about 6 months to 8 years with croup (viral laryngotracheitis) in the emergency department (ED) or clinic: severity grading, red flags for other causes of stridor, oral dexamethasone, nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine), observation, admission and paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) or anaesthesia escalation. Uses the Canadian Paediatric Society (CPS) 2026 practice point, the Children's Minnesota 2025 croup guideline and product labels. Infants under 6 months, recurrent or atypical croup, known airway anomalies and adults are excluded.
learningObjectives: Give dexamethasone to every child with croup.
Use nebulised adrenaline for stridor at rest and observe 2 to 4 hours.
Spot the red flags of epiglottitis, tracheitis and foreign body.
pitfalls: Upsetting the child for unnecessary tests.
Missing epiglottitis in a drooling child without a barky cough.
keyPoints: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg is the mainstay.
Adrenaline dose is the same for all ages.
Quiet stridor with lethargy is a sign of exhaustion, not improvement.

patientEducation: Croup is a viral infection that swells the windpipe; it usually improves in 3 to 7 days.
Return at once for stridor at rest, hard breathing, drooling, blue colour or drowsiness.
Fever medicine helps comfort; steam or mist is not needed.
lifestyleAndDiet: Keep the child calm and upright during coughing episodes.
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician or paediatrician; PICU or anaesthesia for severe cases; ENT for persistent severe or recurrent croup (CPS 2026, Sections Treatment and Other therapies).
dischargeCriteria: No stridor at rest 2 to 4 hours after the last adrenaline dose, saturation normal, drinking, carers understand return advice (CPS 2026, Section Epinephrine).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: General practitioner review if not improving in a few days; outpatient ENT referral for recurrent croup or croup outside the usual age range (CPS 2026, Section Other therapies).
